messages.subject: gravity model (for modeling trade) in stan
parts:
Hi,

Does anybody have experience with such models?  I have tried implementing one in stan but without success - while if works fine with R glm function.

For example, the following R code:
glm(trade ~ exporter + importer + distance - 1, family = "poisson")

Seemingly equivalent stan code doesn't converge:
    for (i in 1 : N) {
        mu [i] <- coeff * distance [i] + A [exporter [i]] + B [importer [i]];
        trade [i] ~ poisson (exp (mu [i]));
    }

Thanks a lot for any help,
Linas

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gravity model (for modeling trade) in stan
parts:
Hi, I have 2 questions:
First, what’s your model for the A’s and the B’s?  The parameterization you’re using could make a difference.
Second, I recommend overdispersed Poisson (for example, negative binomial) rather than Poisson.  If there is overdispersion (and there typically is, in real data), the Poisson likelihood will be too sharp and this can cause computational problems.

Finally, this is yet another motivation for us to implement marginal maximum likelihood:  not just for speed in moderately-large problems, but for compatibility to other software even in small problems.

A

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gravity model (for modeling trade) in stan
parts: If you were going to use the Poisson distribution, it is better in Stan to do

for (i in 1 : N) {
        mu [i] <- coeff * distance [i] + A [exporter [i]] + B [importer [i]];
}

trade ~ poisson_log (mu);

I would agree with Andrew that you should account for the overdispersion, possibly by adding the logarithm of gamma distributed variables to mu[i], perhaps grouped by exporter[i] and importer[i]. From a frequentist perspective, there is an argument for doing Poissons in situations like this where some dyads have zero trade and then doing calculating sandwich standard errors to account for the fact that the assumption that the variance is equal to the expectation is completely wrong. But from a Bayesian perspective, it is just using a dubious likelihood.

Ben

parts:
I can see that in a single case you'd get that.
If y is a vector of N observations from Poisson(lambda),
then the MLE of lambda is hat_lambda = sum(y)/N, which has
the property that sum(y) = hat_lambda * N. See:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution#Maximum_likelihood

For negative binomial, that property only holds if the
overdispersion is zero. See

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution#Maximum_likelihood_estimation

But if the overdispersion isn't zero, then you presumably
don't want to use a misspecified model just because of this
sum property.

Also, if you put a prior on lambda, then the property will
no longer hold of the posterior mode.

Also, I don't think the Bayesian posterior mean will match
the posterior mode, even if the model doesn't use priors or
overdispersion.

- Bob

Here's the Wikipedia page:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity_model_of_trade#Econometric_Estimation_of_Gravity_Equations

which seems largely based on this:

http://www.mitpressjournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1162/rest.88.4.641

Without worrying about overdispersion, I think the model described in
the Wikipedia would look like this in Stan:
for (i in 1:N) {

for (j in 1:N) {
real lambda;
lambda <- b[0]
+ b[1] * log_gdp[i]
+ b[2] * log_gdp[j]
- b[3] * log_distance[i,j];
f[i,j] ~ poisson_log(lambda)
}
}

where log_gdp[i] is the log of the GDP of unit i, log_distance[i,j]
is the log of the distance between the two, and f[i,j] is the volume
of trade from country i to country j.

In Stan, this requires integer-valued f, and integers only go
up to 2^31 or so. Of course, with high counts, the normal's a very
good approximation.

The Poisson gives you a noise term and the conservation you want only
holds in expectation.

I couldn't line up the Wikipedia presentation with yours.

for (i in 1 : N) {
mu [i] <- coeff * distance [i] + A [exporter [i]] + B [importer [i]];
trade [i] ~ poisson (exp (mu [i]));
}

It looks like what you're doing is going to make A and B random
intercepts for each importer and exporter rather than multiplying
each's log GDP by a coefficient.

- Bob

parts:
Yes, I agree that overdispersion might be an issue and thanks for suggesting negative binomial and poisson with extra-poisson variation.  I will certainly try both.  Since all models are wrong and only some are useful the "right" distribution will most probably be chosen based on results.

However, I am not sure how to deal with A [exporter [i]] + B [importer [i]] - those are coefficients of attraction and repulsion for each entity.  Unfortunately the model described in /wiki/Gravity_model_of_trade#Econometric_Estimation_of_Gravity_Equations is slightly different although both models are called gravity models.  The one I would like to implement in stan is described in 'The Poisson quasi-maximum likelihood estimator: a
solution to the ‘adding up’ problem in gravity models', equation 2. I am wondering if having two intercepts A and B are not going to lead to identifiability and if so, how to tackle this.
Thank you,
Linas
On 11/2/2014 10:06 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:

Hi, my guess is that “Without worrying about overdispersion” is a mistake, and that you should worry about overdispersion, otherwise Im guessing you’ll be in trouble.

On Nov 2, 2014, at 9:08 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:


Here's the Wikipedia page:

 http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gravity_model_of_trade#Econometric_Estimation_of_Gravity_Equations

which seems largely based on this:

 http://www.mitpressjournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1162/rest.88.4.641

Without worrying about overdispersion, I think the model described in 
the Wikipedia would look like this in Stan:

   for (i in 1:N) {
     for (j in 1:N) {
       real lambda;
       lambda <- b[0] 
                 + b[1] * log_gdp[i] 
                 + b[2] * log_gdp[j] 
                 - b[3] * log_distance[i,j];
       f[i,j] ~ poisson_log(lambda)
     }
   }

where log_gdp[i] is the log of the GDP of unit i, log_distance[i,j]
is the log of the distance between the two, and f[i,j] is the volume
of trade from country i to country j.

In Stan, this requires integer-valued f, and integers only go
up to 2^31 or so.  Of course, with high counts, the normal's a very
good approximation.

The Poisson gives you a noise term and the conservation you want only
holds in expectation.

I couldn't line up the Wikipedia presentation with yours. 

 for (i in 1 : N) {
   mu [i] <- coeff * distance [i] + A [exporter [i]] + B [importer [i]];
   trade [i] ~ poisson (exp (mu [i]));
 }

It looks like what you're doing is going to make A and B random
intercepts for each importer and exporter rather than multiplying
each's log GDP by a coefficient.

- Bob



On Nov 2, 2014, at 6:40 PM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

Can you then just add a data-level error term, so that the model becomes:
mu [i] <- coeff * distance [i] + A [exporter [i]] + B [importer [i]] + sigma_eta*eta[i];
where then the eta[i]’s have a N(0,1) error distribution?

On Nov 2, 2014, at 6:26 PM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:


Thanks to all for very good suggestions.  However, for this specific case, for any country total export = total import.  I am not comfortable of violating physical constraints.  While I know that Poisson satisfies those constraints it looks for me that negative binomial satisfies those constraints only when overdispersion = 0.  Is violation of physical constraints justified? Can anybody help? Is there an example when relaxing physical constraints leads to a reasonable prediction of some function of exports and imports (such as GDP) for each country?

Thanks,
Linas

On 11/1/2014 4:54 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:

I can see that in a single case you'd get that.
If y is a vector of N observations from Poisson(lambda),
then the MLE of lambda is hat_lambda = sum(y)/N, which has
the property that sum(y) = hat_lambda * N.  See:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution#Maximum_likelihood

For negative binomial, that property only holds if the
overdispersion is zero.  See

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution#Maximum_likelihood_estimation

But if the overdispersion isn't zero, then you presumably
don't want to use a misspecified model just because of this
sum property.

Also, if you put a prior on lambda, then the property will
no longer hold of the posterior mode.

Also, I don't think the Bayesian posterior mean will match
the posterior mode, even if the model doesn't use priors or
overdispersion.

- Bob

Overdispersed Poisson (whether negative binomial or other) can be interpreted as Poisson with an additional data-level error term.  So I can’t imagine that you’d lose any relevant theoretical property by adding overdispersion to your model.

On Nov 1, 2014, at 11:30 AM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:


Ben,

Thank you.  There is some trade conservation property: preserve total trade flows between the actual and estimated bilateral trade matrices.  It is so called 'adding up' problem.  It is expressed as: sum_ij trade_ij = sum_ij trade*_ij where trade* is estimator.  I think one can prove that poisson preserves this.  I am not sure about negative binomial.

Linas

On 11/1/2014 10:41 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

If you were going to use the Poisson distribution, it is better in Stan to do

for (i in 1 : N) {
      mu [i] <- coeff * distance [i] + A [exporter [i]] + B [importer [i]];
}

trade ~ poisson_log (mu);

I would agree with Andrew that you should account for the overdispersion, possibly by adding the logarithm of gamma distributed variables to mu[i], perhaps grouped by exporter[i] and importer[i]. From a frequentist perspective, there is an argument for doing Poissons in situations like this where some dyads have zero trade and then doing calculating sandwich standard errors to account for the fact that the assumption that the variance is equal to the expectation is completely wrong. But from a Bayesian perspective, it is just using a dubious likelihood.

Ben

First, what’s your model for the A’s and the B’s?  The parameterization you’re using could make a difference.

Identifying models with priors may require many samples.

One thing you can try to do is modify some of the warmup parameters.

1. Reduce the stepsize (say to 0.01 or 0.001)
2. Increase the adapt_delta (say to 0.95 or 0.99 or even 0.995)

That should make the runs more consistent, but slower.

Usually when we have a model like this, we'd make A hierarchical.
So rather than
for (i in 1 : N) {

mu[i] <- coeff[1] * pred1[i] +
A[origin[i]] + B[destination[i]] + sigma_eta * eta[i];

with

A ~ normal(10, 5);
B ~ normal(0, 1);

I'd suggest

A ~ normal(mu_A, sigma_A);
mu_A ~ normal(10,5);
sigma_A ~ cauchy(0,5);

I'd do the same thing with the coeff.

Do you really want to set B to normal(0,1)? The 0 mean will
control the location, but the 1 scale may be too restrictive.

- Bob
